medium.titulo: I Installed One AI Chrome Extension – Now I Can’t Imagine Browsing Without It
medium.resumo: The little AI tool sitting inside my browser has changed the way I research, write, summarize, and get things done.
medium.conteudo_html:
The little AI tool sitting inside my browser has changed the way I research, write, summarize, and get things done.

“Sometimes the biggest productivity upgrade isn’t a new computer. It’s one small tool that removes five unnecessary steps.”

Disclaimer:

This article is based on my personal experience and general research about AI browser extensions. Features, pricing, availability, and privacy policies can change, so always check the extension’s current information before installing it.

⸻

I Didn’t Need Another AI Tool

I’ll be honest.

When I first started using AI, I thought I needed to try everything.

New chatbot?

Try it.

New AI writing tool?

Try it.

New productivity app?

Try it.

Eventually, I had a browser full of tabs and a surprisingly simple problem:

I was spending more time switching between AI tools than actually using them.

I would read an interesting article, open another tab, copy the text, paste it into an AI chatbot, wait for the answer, then return to the original page.

It worked.

But it wasn’t exactly efficient.

Then I discovered something that made much more sense to me:

AI directly inside the browser.

Instead of bringing the webpage to AI, I could bring AI to the webpage.

And that small change made a bigger difference than I expected.

⸻

So, What Is an AI Chrome Extension?

Think of a Chrome extension as a small tool that adds extra abilities to your browser.

An AI extension can add things like:

→ Page summaries

→ Writing assistance

→ Translation

→ Research help

→ Email drafting

→ Text rewriting

→ Question answering

→ AI chat inside webpages

Some extensions focus on one task, while others try to become an all-in-one AI assistant.

Recent 2026 comparisons show that tools such as Sider, Monica, Perplexity, Grammarly, Merlin and others are competing in different areas rather than doing exactly the same thing. (Prophet)

That’s why I don’t think there is one extension that is automatically “the best” for everyone.

The best one depends on what you actually do online.

⸻

⭐ The One I’d Try First: Sider

If I wanted an AI extension that could handle several different tasks from one place, Sider would be one of my first options to test.

Why?

Because it works like an AI sidebar inside the browser.

Instead of opening another tab, I can interact with AI while I’m already reading a webpage.

I can use it for things like:

  • Summarizing content
  • * Explaining difficult information
  • * Rewriting selected text
  • * Translating
  • * Asking questions about a page
  • * Working with different AI models

Some current comparisons highlight Sider specifically for its multi-model approach and browser sidebar workflow. (Fastio)

And for me, the biggest advantage isn’t necessarily the number of features.

It’s convenience.

⸻

Imagine You’re Reading a Long Article

Let’s say I open a 20-minute article.

I don’t necessarily want to read every paragraph immediately.

I might want to know:

“What are the three main points?”

Normally, I would copy the article or switch to another tool.

With an AI browser extension, I can ask directly from the page.

That’s the kind of small improvement that doesn’t sound revolutionary.

But when you do it dozens of times, it starts saving real effort.

⸻

🔎 For Research: Perplexity Is Interesting

If your main reason for using AI is research, I’d look closely at Perplexity’s browser experience.

The big attraction is that it focuses heavily on web research and source-backed answers.

Some current guides recommend Perplexity specifically for people who want research help and citations while browsing. (Fastio)

For example, imagine I’m researching a topic for an article.

Instead of opening five different tabs immediately, I can use AI to help me understand the page I’m already reading.

But there’s one rule I always follow:

AI-generated research still needs verification.

An AI answer can sound incredibly confident and still be wrong.

So I use it to speed up research – not to turn off my brain.

⸻

✍️ For Writing: Grammarly Still Has A Place

When people hear “AI,” they often think about generating entire articles.

But sometimes I don’t need AI to write for me.

I just need it to tell me:

“This sentence doesn’t sound right.”

That’s where Grammarly remains useful.

It can provide grammar, spelling, clarity and tone assistance directly in browser text fields, and its AI features add rewriting support. (Fastio)

This is particularly useful for:

Emails.

Social media posts.

Online applications.

Blog posts.

Comments.

Professional messages.

For someone who writes regularly, having suggestions appear where you’re already typing can be much easier than copying everything into another application.

⸻

🧠 The Real Benefit Is Not “AI”

Here’s something I realized.

The biggest benefit of these extensions isn’t actually artificial intelligence.

It’s context.

When AI is sitting inside the webpage I’m already using, I don’t have to constantly explain what I’m looking at.

That’s important.

Imagine you’re reading a complicated article.

You highlight one paragraph and ask:

“Explain this like I’m a beginner.”

That’s much easier than copying the paragraph, opening another tab, pasting it, writing the prompt, and returning to the original page.

One small action replaces several.

And productivity is often just that:

Removing unnecessary steps.

⸻

📧 What About Emails?

This is another area where browser AI can be useful.

Imagine opening your inbox and seeing a long email.

You understand the message, but you’re not sure how to respond.

An AI writing assistant can help create a first draft or adjust the tone.

You could ask for:

Professional

Friendly

Short

Polite

More confident

But I wouldn’t send an AI-generated email without reading it first.

Because sometimes AI produces something that is technically correct but sounds like it was written by a company CEO from a different planet.

😂

Human review still matters.

⸻

⚠️ But There Is Something You Should Check First

Before installing any AI browser extension, I think there’s one thing people should pay more attention to:

Permissions.

An extension may need access to webpage content to perform its job.

That doesn’t automatically make it unsafe.

But you should understand what you’re installing.

Some recent 2026 guides specifically warn users to examine extension permissions and privacy practices before installing AI tools. (Fastio)

Ask yourself:

What information can this extension access?

Does it need access to every website?

What does its privacy policy say?

Who operates it?

Does it handle sensitive information?

This becomes especially important if you’re working with:

  • Banking information
  • * Passwords
  • * Private documents
  • * Client information
  • * Personal messages
  • * Confidential work

Convenience is great.

But privacy is more important.

⸻

🚫 Don’t Install 15 AI Extensions

This is another mistake I almost made.

I used to think:

“If one AI extension helps, five must be even better.”

No.

Eventually your browser becomes a Christmas tree.

Icons everywhere.

Notifications everywhere.

Suggestions everywhere.

And suddenly you’re spending more time managing your tools than doing your work.

I prefer a simple setup now.

One extension for writing.

One for research.

Maybe one additional tool for a specific workflow.

That’s enough for most people.

⸻

My Simple AI Browser Workflow

If I were starting again, I’d keep it simple.

STEP 1 – Browse Normally

Don’t change how you work.

STEP 2 – Find Something Useful

An article, email, document or webpage.

STEP 3 – Ask AI For Help

Summarize it.

Explain it.

Rewrite it.

Translate it.

Research it.

STEP 4 – Verify Important Information

Especially facts, numbers and claims.

STEP 5 – Use Your Own Judgment

AI gives you assistance.

You make the final decision.

That’s it.

⸻

AI Should Save Time – Not Create More Work

This is probably the biggest lesson I’ve learned.

Sometimes people download an AI tool because they want to become more productive.

Then they spend two hours learning the tool.

Then another hour customizing it.

Then they forget what they originally wanted to accomplish.

That’s backwards.

The tool should solve a problem.

Not become the problem.

If an extension saves you time, keep it.

If it makes your workflow more complicated, remove it.

Simple.

⸻

The Future of Browsing Might Feel Very Different

We’re already moving away from the idea that a browser is just a place where we open websites.

The browser is becoming a workspace.

We research there.

Write there.

Study there.

Shop there.

Work there.

Communicate there.

So it makes sense that AI is moving into the browser too.

Instead of:

Website → Copy → New tab → AI → Paste → Answer → Back to website

the experience becomes:

Website → AI → Done

That sounds like a tiny change.

But tiny changes repeated every day can become huge productivity gains.

⸻

Final Thoughts

I don’t think everyone needs an AI Chrome extension.

If you only browse casually, you might never need one.

But if you spend hours every day researching, writing, studying, emailing or creating content online, an AI extension can be surprisingly useful.

For an all-in-one browser assistant, I’d look at tools such as Sider or Monica.

For research, Perplexity is worth exploring.

For writing and editing, Grammarly remains a strong option.

And if you’re already using another AI tool that fits your workflow, there’s no reason to switch just because something is trending. (Prophet)

The point isn’t to collect AI tools.

The point is to find one tool that removes one annoying part of your day.

Because sometimes productivity doesn’t come from working harder.

It comes from eliminating the little things that keep interrupting you.

And now I’m curious:

If you could add ONE AI superpower to your Chrome browser, what would you want it to do?

medium.resumo: Real screenshots of every step, the exact prompt, and the clip it made
medium.conteudo_html:
Real screenshots of every step, the exact prompt, and the clip it made

I wrote this with AI assistance (Claude) and checked every step against the live page this morning. The screenshots are real; the clips are unedited model output, shown here as stills.

I’m Louis Chi, and I work on RefVid, a tool that turns a few photos of the same person or product into short AI videos. Yesterday our first paying customer arrived on one of our guide pages and went from landing to paying in about four minutes, before making a single video. The lesson for me was simple: the page someone lands on has to do the job by itself. No “go to the studio and figure it out.”

So here is the whole flow on our free AI video generator page, one screenshot per step, using three photos of a sneaker.

1. Open the page and pick a starting point

The first screen, signed out. The row is templates; the box underneath is the generator.

The row at the top is a set of ready-made scenes: a 360° turntable, a floating product, a water splash, an unboxing, a morning routine and more. Clicking Use on one fills the box below with its prompt. The page starts on Product 360, a slow turntable spin on a grey studio background, which is what I wanted.

You don’t have to use a template. You can delete the text and write one line of your own.

2. Add a few photos of the same thing

Three photos added. Each one can be removed with its ×, and the + adds more.

Click Reference and add one to five photos of your subject. I used three: the side, a three-quarter view from the front, and the back with the heel tab. The sneaker, AERO 1, is a product we made up for demos; it doesn’t exist.

Why more than one photo? The model is drawing the whole scene again. If it has only seen the front, it has to guess the back. Three angles gave it the heel, the orange panel and the label, so it didn’t need to invent them. One sharp, well-lit photo is enough to start; three to five are better.

3. Check the words, the model and the settings

The model list, opened from the box. Each model has one line on what it’s good at.

The template’s prompt says “your product” instead of a name, so it works for whatever you upload:

Your product on a round white turntable in a photo studio, rotating slowly through a full 360 degrees, light grey seamless background, soft even studio light, locked-off camera, sharp focus on every detail.

Under it sit three controls: the model (Kling 3.0 Omni by default; eight models in the list), the shape and length (1:1, 5 seconds, 720p, one version) and a Sound switch, off here. I left all of them alone. Those defaults are what the free first video covers. Improve in the corner rewrites a short idea into a fuller prompt if you’d rather start from your own words.

4. Press Generate and sign in

Signed out, Generate opens this sheet over the page. Your photos and words stay in the box.

Signed out, Generate asks you to sign in with Google or with a 6-digit code sent by email. No card. After signing in you come back to the same page, and the clip starts with the same photos and the same words; you don’t type anything twice. It’s made right there in the page, and the finished clip plays in place with Download and Open in studio. A clip usually takes 2 to 10 minutes, and you get an email when it’s ready.

I didn’t press it through this morning, because this exact template has an example made from these exact three photos. That example is below.

5. What three photos turned into

Top: the three photos. Bottom: four frames from the 5-second clip, Kling 3.0 Omni, square, no sound, not edited.

The shoe turns through a full circle and the details hold: the knit pattern, the orange heel panel, the AERO 1 print, the white sole. The back of the shoe comes from photo three rather than from the model’s imagination. You can watch the moving version on the Product 360 template page.

The same thing works for people. These are four photos of Mia, an invented person, and two separate 5-second clips made from them:

Four photos of Mia, then two clips made from them on the free clip’s default settings. Not edited.

The trail clip’s prompt starts like this: “Mia hikes along a narrow mountain trail through drifting mist and tall pine trees, then stops and turns to look back over her shoulder toward the camera with a slight smile.” The face, the bob and the jacket come from the photos, so the next clip starts from the same person without uploading again.

What I’d tell a friend before trying it

  • Use photos you have the right to use: yourself, people who agreed, products you own or sell.
  • Five seconds is one action and one camera move. “Spins on a turntable” works. “Spins, then flies to a beach, then a hand picks it up” doesn’t.
  • Watch the result at full size before you post it. Hands, faces and small text on labels are where AI video still slips. A picture is redrawn, not pasted.
  • The free part is the first video, 5 seconds on the defaults. It downloads as a plain MP4 with no watermark, and commercial use is allowed. After that, videos use paid credits.

If you’d rather mix different pictures in one clip, say a room, a mood board and a product, each in a shot you choose, that’s the images to video AI page. For one subject from a few photos, the free generator page is the shortest way I know.

Louis Chi works on RefVid.

medium.titulo: Several LLMs on One Machine: One Folder, Unisex Skills
medium.resumo: Say you have Claude, and Claude Code of course. And you know where to switch between Claude and Claude Code.
medium.conteudo_html:
Say you have Claude, and Claude Code of course. And you know where to switch between Claude and Claude Code.

A friend and I once spent five minutes looking for that switch. Five minutes, two people who use this thing every day. Imagine how much Anthropic undersells its own product, given that they simply hid the switch between ordinary Claude and Claude Code. Most people who are not deep in this will never find it.

Fine, that is not the point. The point is what happens when you stop having one AI on your computer and start having several.

What actually sits on one machine

On my machine there is Antigravity. Antigravity is a convenient interface for reaching Google’s artificial intelligence, the one called Gemini.

There is Codex, which lives in the same application as ChatGPT. At least that one has convenient switches.

And there is Claude, which switches over to Claude Code.

Three vendors, three different products, three different ideas of how you should work. Left alone, each of them behaves as if it is the only one in the room. One writes a file, another does not know it exists. One learns how to do something, the other starts from zero.

One folder, or folders with instructions

For all of them to work in symbiosis with each other, they need to work out of one folder.

Or out of several folders, but then every folder has to carry a strict instruction: what it is for, what lives inside, and how to handle it. An LLM that walks into a folder with no explanation will guess. An LLM that walks into a folder with a clear instruction will do what you meant.

This sounds like housekeeping, and it is. But it is the housekeeping that decides whether three models share a workspace or fight over it.

Unisex skills

The second part is the skills, the abilities you teach them.

I build all my skills unisex. A skill is not invented only for Claude or only for Codex. It is written so that any LLM that gets access to it knows how to use it.

In practice a skill is simply an instruction, in Russian and English. A fairly detailed one, naturally: how an LLM uses some piece of functionality and what to do step by step.

Loosely speaking, take Telegram. The skill says: here are your login and password, here is access to the Telethon library or an MCP, here is how you read a chat, here is how you send a message, and so on. Claude reads it and works. Codex reads the same file and works. Gemini reads it and works. Nobody needs their own copy.

What you get

So several LLMs from different vendors can run on one machine perfectly well. They can avoid stepping on each other, use one shared memory, one set of unisex skills.

And two things follow from that.

You save on tokens, because the work does not all have to go through the most expensive model. A task that a cheaper model handles fine goes to the cheaper model.

And you distribute tasks across several LLMs in parallel. While one is busy, another picks up the next job, from the same folder, with the same instructions, with the same memory.

Over to you

If you want the details, or want me to help you build something like this, write in the comments.

As you remember, I am trying to get a job at an AI lab. And I need cases where I helped somebody set something up. Glad to be useful.

And I am waiting for your comments too: how have you set yours up? Glad to hear it.

medium.titulo: Nuxt 前端框架，還有 Server Middleware？從 HTTP 安全標頭開始和 nosniff
medium.resumo: 使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫
medium.conteudo_html:
使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫

最近在處理 Nuxt 網站的安全性設定時

Nuxt 明明是前端框架

卻可以透過 server/middleware 修改伺服器回傳的 HTTP Header？

原來 Nuxt 不只是 Vue 的前端開發工具，它也具備伺服器端的執行能力

Nuxt 不只是前端框架

在一般 Vue SPA（Single Page Application）中

伺服器主要提供 HTML、CSS 和 JavaScript 檔案

瀏覽器下載後，再由 JavaScript 產生畫面

Nuxt 則支援 SSR（Server-Side Rendering，伺服器端渲染）。

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  ssr: true
})

當 SSR 啟用時

Nuxt 可以先在伺服器執行 Vue 程式、產生 HTML，再傳送給瀏覽器。

瀏覽器收到 HTML 後，會再透過 JavaScript 接手互動功能

這個過程稱為 Hydration。

因此 Nuxt 的程式可能在兩個不同環境執行：

  • Server（伺服器）：產生 HTML、處理 HTTP 請求。
  • Client（瀏覽器）：呈現畫面、處理使用者互動。

Nuxt 使用的伺服器引擎叫做 Nitro

它可以處理 SSR、Server API 和 Server Middleware。

Middleware 是什麼？

Middleware 中文稱為「中介軟體」。

可以把它想成辦公大樓的警衛。

當有人準備進入辦公室時，警衛會先檢查身分，確認符合條件才讓他進去。

Middleware 也是類似的概念

在主要處理流程之前，先執行某些工作。

Nuxt 有兩種容易搞混的 Middleware。

Route Middleware

放在：middleware/

主要處理頁面導航

例如檢查使用者是否登入。

export default defineNuxtRouteMiddleware((to) => {
  const isLoggedIn = false

  if (!isLoggedIn && to.path !== '/login') {
    return navigateTo('/login')
  }
})

Server Middleware

放在：server/middleware/

主要處理進入 Nitro 的 HTTP 請求

例如記錄請求資訊、設定 HTTP Response Header。

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(event, 'X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')
})

兩者最大的差別是：

  • Route Middleware：處理使用者要前往哪個頁面。
  • Server Middleware：處理伺服器收到的 HTTP 請求。

為什麼需要 X-Content-Type-Options？

當瀏覽器向伺服器索取檔案時

伺服器會透過 Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器檔案類型。

Content-Type: text/html
Content-Type: application/javascript
Content-Type: text/css

但某些情況下，瀏覽器可能根據檔案內容自行猜測類型。

這種行為稱為 MIME Sniffing。

伺服器回傳：

Content-Type: text/plain

但檔案內容卻是：

alert("Hello!")

伺服器宣告這是普通文字，但內容看起來像 JavaScript。

如果瀏覽器在載入腳本時自行猜測類型並執行，就可能增加安全風險。

因此可以設定：

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

要求瀏覽器在載入 JavaScript、CSS 等資源時，遵守對應的 MIME 類型檢查。

如果宣告的類型不符合要求，瀏覽器就會阻擋載入，而不是自行猜測後繼續使用。

使用 Server Middleware 設定安全標頭

在 Nuxt 專案建立：

server/middleware/security-headers.ts

import {
  defineEventHandler,
  setResponseHeader
} from 'h3'

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(
    event,
    'X-Content-Type-Options',
    'nosniff'
  )
})

這段程式其實只做一件事情：

在 Nuxt 伺服器處理 HTTP 請求時，替回應加入 X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff。

逐行來看：

  • defineEventHandler()：建立一個 HTTP 請求處理函式。
  • event：代表這次 HTTP 請求與回應的相關資訊。
  • setResponseHeader()：替 HTTP 回應設定 Header。
  • X-Content-Type-Options：安全標頭名稱。
  • nosniff：要求瀏覽器遵守對應資源的 MIME 類型限制。

因為檔案放在 server/middleware/，Nuxt 會自動註冊這段程式。

不需要在每個 Vue 頁面重複設定。

不過要注意，這個 Middleware 只能影響經過 Nitro 處理的 HTTP 回應。

如果正式環境還有 IIS、Nginx 或其他 Web Server 直接提供檔案，就需要另外確認。

如何驗證設定成功？

啟動 Nuxt 專案後，可以使用 Chrome 開發者工具確認。

  1. 按下 F12 開啟 DevTools。
  2. 選擇 Network。
  3. 重新整理網頁。
  4. 點選網頁的 Document 請求。
  5. 查看 Response Headers。
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html;charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

這代表目前檢查的 HTTP 回應已經包含安全標頭。

另外，也應檢查 JavaScript 和 CSS 是否具有正確的 Content-Type

避免新增 nosniff 後造成檔案載入失敗。

重點整理

  • Nuxt 不只是前端工具，也具備透過 Nitro 執行伺服器端程式的能力。
  • SSR 可以在伺服器先產生 HTML，再交由瀏覽器接手互動。
  • Route Middleware 負責頁面導航與路由檢查。
  • Server Middleware 負責 Nuxt 伺服器端的 HTTP 請求處理。
  • Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器回應內容的類型。
  • MIME Sniffing 是瀏覽器根據內容自行判斷檔案類型的行為。
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff 可以降低特定資源因 MIME 類型錯誤判斷而產生的安全風險。
  • 設定完成後，仍需要檢查 HTTP 回應，確認標頭確實生效。

medium.titulo: Why Do We Even Need React, Vue and Angular? 6 Things They Do So You Don’t Have To
medium.resumo: In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself.
medium.conteudo_html:
In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself. What they add is knowing when to call them, which ones to use, and which calls to skip.

Open the source of React, Vue or Angular and you won’t find any browser magic. They create elements with document.createElement, change text with nodeValue and textContent, and attach listeners with addEventListener, exactly like you would in a plain .js file.

So why does almost every team reach for one of them? It isn’t because the DOM is slow or because vanilla JavaScript can’t build a real app. These libraries make a long list of small decisions for you, on every click, and they get them right every time. You would get most of them right too, at least on the first day. By month six, with three teammates and forty screens, you’d be getting them wrong.

Here are the six that matter most. I checked each one against the shipped source of React 19.3, Vue 3.5 and Angular 21.2, and measured the browser side in Chrome 156. The interactive version of this post, with live demos you can run in your browser, is on allahabadi.dev.

1. You stop updating the screen by hand

This is the big one, and every other point in this post sits on top of it.

Take a small shopping cart. A cart icon shows a count, a list shows the items, a line shows the total, and the checkout button says how many items you’re buying. Four places on the screen show the same piece of data.

Without a library, every action has to remember every place:

<span id="badge">0</span>
<ul id="list"></ul>
<b id="total">0</b>
<button id="checkout">Checkout (0)</button>
const cart = [];
const badge = document.querySelector('#badge');
const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const total = document.querySelector('#total');
const checkout = document.querySelector('#checkout');
function addItem(item) {
  cart.push(item);
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = `${item.name} ₹${item.price}`;
  list.append(li);
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function removeLast() {
  cart.pop();
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.lastElementChild?.remove();
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  // checkout.textContent was never updated here
}

Nothing in that code crashes. removeLast just forgets the checkout button, so after you remove an item the button still says the old number. No error shows up in the console, and no test fails unless someone wrote one for that exact label. A real app has hundreds of these "update these four things" functions, and each new feature adds one more place each of them has to remember.

The fix is to flip the direction. Instead of writing “when this happens, change these elements”, you write one function that says what the screen should look like for any cart, and you call it after every change:

let cart = [];
function render() {
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.replaceChildren(...cart.map((i) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `${i.name} ₹${i.price}`;
    return li;
  }));
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function addItem(item) { cart = [...cart, item]; render(); }
function removeLast() { cart = cart.slice(0, -1); render(); }

(It uses the same four const elements as the first snippet.) Now no action can forget the button, because no action touches the screen at all. They change the data, and render draws the screen from it. People describe this as UI is a function of state: same state in, same screen out.

That is the whole idea React, Vue and Angular are built on. In React the same cart looks like this:

import { useState } from 'react';
export function Cart() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
  const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  return (
    <>
      <span>{cart.length}</span>
      <ul>
        {cart.map((i, n) => <li key={n}>{i.name} ₹{i.price}</li>)}
      </ul>
      <b>{total}</b>
      <button onClick={() => setCart([...cart, { name: 'Tea', price: 40 }])}>Add tea</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCart(cart.slice(0, -1))}>Remove last</button>
      <button>Checkout ({cart.length})</button>
    </>
  );
}

But my vanilla render() has a cost the React version doesn't. It rebuilds the whole list on every click, even when only one item changed. Do that on a list of 2,000 rows and the browser throws away 2,000 elements and builds 2,000 new ones to change one price. Doing "render from state" without paying that price is the actual work these libraries do, and the next three sections are about how they do it.

2. They pick the right moment to touch the DOM

A browser tab runs your JavaScript and draws the page on the same thread. It can’t paint while your code is running. Roughly, one turn of the loop looks like this: run a task (your click handler), run the microtasks queued during it, run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then recalculate styles, lay the page out and paint.

When you change the DOM directly, the change happens right there, in the middle of your handler. When you then read something that depends on layout (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), innerText), the browser has to stop and lay the page out right now, because the layout it has is out of date. Do that in a loop and you get one full layout per pass. This has a name: layout thrashing.

const rows = document.querySelectorAll('.row');
const heights = [];
for (const row of rows) {
  row.textContent = 'Read';        // write: layout is now out of date
  heights.push(row.offsetHeight);  // read: browser must lay out right now
}

The libraries never write to the DOM the moment you change state. They write it down and do all the DOM work later, in one go:

  • React collects every setState call made during an event. If your click handler calls setName, setCity and setAge, React renders once and commits once, after your handler returns and before the browser paints. Work that isn't urgent, like a startTransition update, goes through React's scheduler, which posts its work with MessageChannel and gives the main thread back every 5 ms so a keypress doesn't have to wait for a long render.
  • Vue puts each component that needs updating in a queue and flushes the whole queue in one microtask (Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs)). That is why you need await nextTick() to see the updated DOM right after changing state.
  • Angular in zoneless mode schedules change detection with whichever fires first, a setTimeout or a requestAnimationFrame, so a burst of changes in one handler leads to one check.

The core of the trick fits in six lines:

let queued = false;
function scheduleRender(render) {
  if (queued) return;
  queued = true;
  queueMicrotask(() => { queued = false; render(); });
}

Call scheduleRender(render) ten times in one click and render runs once.

One correction to something you’ll often read: none of the three uses requestIdleCallback to apply your updates. An idle callback can be delayed for a long time, and an update needs to be on screen in the next frame. Vue uses it for hydrateOnIdle, and Angular for @defer (on idle) blocks. Both are cases where waiting is fine.

You can do all of this by hand. You’d have to know that layout reads in a loop are expensive, that a microtask runs before the next paint, and that requestAnimationFrame exists. Then you'd have to make sure every developer on the team knows it as well, in every file.

3. They choose the fast DOM API for you

The DOM often gives you two ways to do the same thing, and one of them costs a lot more. The best-known pair is textContent and innerText.

textContent joins up the text nodes inside an element. It never looks at CSS. innerText returns the text as it appears on screen: it leaves out elements hidden with CSS, applies text-transform, and turns line boxes into line breaks. To know what is on screen, the browser needs up-to-date styles and layout. So reading innerText right after you changed something forces a full layout.

Writing is a different story, and this is where the usual advice gets it half wrong. In my traces, setting innerText did not force layout. It cost about the same as setting textContent. The only difference is that the innerText setter turns \n into <br> elements. The expensive part is reading it.

The read is easy to put in a hot loop without noticing, like this search filter:

const query = 'error';
for (const row of document.querySelectorAll('.row')) {
  row.hidden = !row.innerText.includes(query);
}

Setting row.hidden makes the layout out of date, and the next row's innerText needs it to be current, so the browser lays the page out again for every row. Swap innerText for textContent and that loop doesn't do any layout until the frame is painted.

Here is how React sets text on an element, from react-dom 19.3 (lightly reformatted):

function setTextContent(node, text) {
  if (text) {
    var firstChild = node.firstChild;
    if (firstChild && firstChild === node.lastChild && 3 === firstChild.nodeType) {
      firstChild.nodeValue = text;
      return;
    }
  }
  node.textContent = text;
}

If the element already holds exactly one text node, React changes that node’s nodeValue in place, which is the cheapest text write the DOM has. Otherwise it uses textContent. innerText doesn't appear anywhere in that path.

Most of the time, these libraries don’t read the DOM at all. The current cart, the current name and the current filter all live in JavaScript, in React’s fibers, Vue’s reactive objects or Angular’s views. When your code reads row.innerText to find out what a row says, it asks the browser to work it out from the page. A library already knows, because it rendered that row. Fewer reads means fewer chances to force layout, and you don't need to remember which layout-reading APIs are dangerous. I measured more than 40 of them in another post.

They skip updates that change nothing

Say a price on the screen is 499, and your code sets it to 499 again. Nothing on screen changes. Does the browser notice?

I tested it in Chrome 156 on a page with 3,000 paragraphs. Each test wrote the same value 200 times and read offsetWidth after each write, the way real code often measures right after updating:

  • el.textContent = '499' (same value): 200 layouts. textContent replaces the child text node with a brand new one every time, so the browser treats it as new content.
  • el.innerHTML = '499' (same value): 200 layouts, for the same reason, plus an HTML parse each time.
  • textNode.nodeValue = '499' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome sees that nothing changed. A MutationObserver still received all 200 records, though.
  • el.style.width = '50px' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome skips an identical inline style too.
  • if (el.textContent !== '499') el.textContent = '499': 0 layouts, 0 mutations.

So the browser skips some identical writes and redoes others, and the two most common ways of setting text are the ones it redoes. You’d have to know which is which.

const price = document.querySelector('#price');
for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
  price.textContent = '499';
  price.offsetWidth;
}

All three libraries put the check in front of the DOM, so they never need that list:

  • React compares old and new text before it marks a text node for update (current.memoizedProps !== newProps). One level up, if you call setCount(5) while the count is already 5, Object.is says nothing changed and React can skip rendering that component altogether.
  • Vue’s reactive setter runs hasChanged(value, oldValue) first. Assigning the same value to a ref doesn't trigger anything that depends on it.
  • Angular compares every template binding to its previous value with Object.is (bindingUpdated) and only touches the DOM when it differs.

All three compare with Object.is, so they check "is it the same value", not "does it look the same":

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
Object.is(user, user);              // true:  update skipped
Object.is(user, { name: 'Asha' });  // false: treated as a change

That is why in React you create a new object to trigger an update, and why a new object built on every render can cause updates you didn’t expect.

5. They treat text as text

This is the reason I’d add to the list. It saves teams from a whole class of security bugs without anyone thinking about it.

When you build UI by hand, the quick way to put a value into a page is innerHTML. It parses whatever string you give it as HTML. If that string came from a user, the user can write HTML into your page, including elements with event handlers that run their JavaScript under your domain. That attack is called cross-site scripting, or XSS.

const greeting = document.querySelector('#greeting');
const name = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('name') ?? '';
greeting.innerHTML = `Hi ${name}`;    // parses name as HTML
greeting.textContent = `Hi ${name}`;  // shows name as plain text

In React, <p>Hi {name}</p> always produces a text node, whatever name holds. Vue's {{ name }} and Angular's {{ name }} work the same way. To put raw HTML on the page you have to ask for it by name: React calls it dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue calls it v-html, and Angular runs anything bound to [innerHTML] through its sanitizer first. The safe way is the default, and the unsafe way is the one you have to go looking for.

6. They make a big codebase easier to work in

The first five points are things the library does at runtime. This one is about the people writing the code, and on a large team it may matter most of all.

  • Components. A <PriceTag> is written once, used in forty places, and changed in one file. With plain DOM code, "reuse" usually means copying a function and its HTML string into another file.
  • Clean-up has a home. Listeners you attach in the template (onClick, @click, (click)) are removed for you when the component goes away, and each library gives you one obvious place for the rest: the useEffect clean-up in React, onUnmounted in Vue, DestroyRef in Angular. By hand, every removeEventListener is yours to remember, and a forgotten one keeps the old element and everything it refers to in memory.
  • Tools that understand your app. React DevTools, Vue DevTools and Angular DevTools show your components and their current state, not just a tree of divs. Hot reload swaps an edited component while the page keeps running, often without losing what you typed into a form.
  • The editor catches mistakes. TypeScript checks JSX and Angular templates, so a misspelled prop or a wrong type shows up as you type, not as a blank screen.
  • A shared map. Routing, forms, data fetching and tests have well-known answers in each ecosystem. A new teammate who knows React already knows where state lives in your app and how a screen gets drawn. Hand-written DOM code is different in every company, and sometimes in every file.

When plain JavaScript is enough

None of this means every page needs a framework. This site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework at all. A blog post, a landing page, or a form with a couple of toggles has very little state and only a few places that show it, so the bugs from the first section rarely have room to happen.

A simple rule of thumb: reach for a library when the same data shows up in several parts of the screen and changes often. That’s where updating by hand starts to break, and where batching, skipping and safe defaults pay for the JavaScript you ship. Below that point, a few addEventListener calls and textContent are perfectly fine.

React, Vue and Angular are still DOM code. They call the same APIs you can. The difference is that they pick the moment, pick the cheap method, skip the pointless call and escape the dangerous string on every update, including the ones nobody on your team thought about.

All five demos (the two carts, the batching race, the innerText filter, the same-value counter and the innerHTML parser) run live here: https://allahabadi.dev/blogs/frontend/why-we-need-react-vue-angular/

corrida_no_ar.titulo: HISTÓRICO! Andreas Almgren FAZ HISTÓRIA em NOVA YORK
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Andreas Almgren quebra jejum de 18 anos e vence a Maratona de Nova York. Em Aracaju, a prova se mantém como a maior do Nordeste por apenas 14 corredores e entrega as primeiras mandalas do Circuito Brasil Gigante. Confira a análise completa dos dois eventos.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Segunda-feira | 2 de novembro de 2026

O sueco Andreas Almgren confirmou seu status de principal atleta não africano do momento ao vencer a Maratona de Nova York em sua estreia na distância. Com um tempo de 2:06:01, ele se tornou o primeiro corredor não nascido na África a conquistar a prova desde 2008, quando o brasileiro Marilson Gomes dos Santos foi campeão. Aos 29 anos, Almgren adiciona essa vitória a um currículo que já inclui o título de campeão mundial de meia maratona, o recorde europeu da mesma distância (58:06) e o título de campeão europeu dos 10.000 metros. O pódio masculino foi completado pelo italiano Yeman Crippa, de origem etíope, com 2:06:14, e por Kamohelo Mofolo, de Lesoto, com 2:06:26. Um detalhe interessante foi a diversidade de tênis no pódio: Almgren usou o Nike Apex, Crippa o On Cloudboom Strike 2, e Mofolo correu com o modelo chinês Xtep 160X 8.0 Pro.

Bicampeonato no feminino em Nova York

Na prova feminina, a queniana Sheila Chepkirui se tornou bicampeã da Maratona de Nova York. Vencedora também em 2024, ela cruzou a linha de chegada com o tempo de 2:24:36. A segunda posição ficou com a norte-americana Jessica McClain, que completou a prova em 2:24:42. McClain tem uma história de superação: ex-corredora de pista, ela chegou a abandonar a carreira por conta da pressão, trabalhou em um emprego convencional e retornou ao esporte de alto rendimento. Apenas um segundo atrás, a queniana Hellen Obiri, campeã em Boston, ficou com o terceiro lugar, marcando 2:24:43.

Maratona de Aracaju: festa, polêmica e a maior do Nordeste (por pouco)

A Maratona de Aracaju 2026 consolidou seu crescimento, mas não sem pontos a serem ajustados. No masculino, a vitória ficou com o sergipano João Marcos Santos, que se tornou bicampeão com o tempo de 2:25:33. Luanderson de Jesus (2:28:33) e Tiago dos Santos Costa (2:35:01) completaram o pódio. Já no feminino, a vencedora foi Taís Ribeiro Vieira, com 3:08:20, seguida por Maísa Santos Fonseca (3:20:31) e Alexandra Freire (3:20:56). A prova não contou com uma categoria de elite feminina, o que gerou críticas. Com 1.951 concluintes na maratona, um aumento de 42% em relação ao ano anterior, a prova se manteve como a maior do Nordeste por uma margem de apenas 14 corredores sobre a Maratona de Fortaleza. Apesar da festa, alguns problemas estruturais foram apontados: a entrega de kits na sexta-feira teve filas de até três horas; a largada apresentou um afunilamento perigoso logo nos primeiros 100 metros, evidenciando a necessidade de largadas em ondas; e houve relatos de falta de água em alguns postos de hidratação, algo inaceitável em provas longas e quentes. Por outro lado, a organização foi elogiada por diversos pontos positivos: a organização dos banheiros na largada, com distribuição de papel higiênico e álcool gel; o espetacular pórtico de largada com show de fogos; a farta hidratação com água a cada 2 km, isotônicos, esponjas e até Coca-Cola; e o novo percurso, que reduziu o trecho de sol intenso na orla. O pós-prova é, sem dúvida, o melhor do Brasil, transformando a chegada em uma grande festa com várias bandas, que segura os corredores por horas.

As primeiras mandalas do Brasil Gigante são entregues

A Maratona de Aracaju foi palco de um momento histórico: a entrega das três primeiras mandalas do Circuito Brasil Gigante. O circuito, um projeto que visa incentivar a participação nas principais maratonas do país, premiou os primeiros atletas a completarem as oito provas que compõem o desafio: Aracaju, Internacional do Paraná, São Paulo, Porto Alegre, Campo Grande, Floripa, Salvador e João Pessoa. Os pioneiros a receber a honraria foram Júnior de Assunção (Bahia), Luciano Meirelles (João Pessoa) e Alexsandro. O projeto, que começou em abril, já conta com 5.975 atletas cadastrados e não tem limite de tempo para ser concluído. Para participar, basta se cadastrar no site oficial em circuitobrasilgigante.com.br.
